One data center. One of America’s driest states. 3,700 formal water protests. Mermaids at the state Capitol. A TV investor blaming China. A mother with her infant son standing in the heat saying “we can’t get this back.”

And Congress — doing absolutely nothing.

This is the story of Utah versus the Stratos Project. And it is the most dramatic, most emotional, most consequential data center battle happening anywhere in America right now.

Published June 11, 2026 by Roll Call. 100% real. 100% verified. And it is exploding across the internet today.

🏜️ WHAT IS THE STRATOS PROJECT — AND WHY IS IT UNLIKE ANYTHING AMERICA HAS SEEN BEFORE

The Stratos Project is a proposed AI data center development in Box Elder County, Utah — a rural, remote stretch of desert in the northwestern corner of one of America’s driest states.

At its original proposed scale — the project would have covered 40,000 acres. That is larger than Bryce Canyon National Park. Larger than the entire city of Washington D.C. One of the most famous natural landscapes in all of America — in a state that is already starving for water.

Residents from a state starving for water have become the face of local struggles against Big Tech, locked in protests against a proposed data center that at one point was set to sprawl thousands of acres larger than its infamous Bryce Canyon. ￼

40,000 acres of Utah desert. Earmarked for an AI data center campus. In a state with one of the most severe water crises in the entire country.

And nobody asked the people of Utah first.

💧 THE WATER NUMBERS THAT EXPLAIN EVERYTHING

Here is the detail that ignited this entire fight — and that makes every Utahn’s blood run cold.

The developers were originally seeking 13,000 acre-feet of rights to groundwater in Utah. ￼ One acre-foot of water equals 325,851 gallons. 13,000 acre-feet equals more than 4.2 BILLION gallons of groundwater — from one of the driest states in America.

And the electricity demand was even more staggering. While developers say Stratos wouldn’t rely on Utah’s existing electric grid — it was once proposed to use more than double the electricity currently consumed by the entire state. ￼

More than double the electricity consumption of the entire state of Utah. For one data center campus. In a desert.

The proposed mega data center needs to change a water right from agricultural to industrial use. Opponents want to prevent that from happening. ￼

Agricultural water — water that feeds Utah’s farms, its communities, its livestock — being redirected to cool AI servers. That is the trade Utah was being asked to make.

😤 THE MOMENT THAT MADE UTAH EXPLODE — A VOTE WITH NO PUBLIC COMMENT

The fury in Utah did not build slowly. It erupted the moment people found out what their government had done without them.

On April 24, the appointed, seven-member board of Utah’s Military Installation Development Authority, or MIDA, gave its approval for the proposal. Ten days later, Box Elder County commissioners voted to keep it moving forward during a tense meeting where protesters shouted in opposition. The commission did not take public comment before voting on May 4. ￼

Read that again. The commission did not take public comment. Before voting on one of the largest development proposals in Utah’s history. A project larger than Bryce Canyon. Using billions of gallons of groundwater. And the public was not allowed to speak.

“Utahns do not feel heard,” Jayden Weekes of Cache County said from a podium at the rally Thursday, balancing one of her young children on her hip. ￼

A mother. A baby on her hip. At a rally at the state Capitol. Because her government voted on a 40,000-acre project and did not let her speak.

🧜 THE IMAGE THAT WENT AROUND THE WORLD — MERMAIDS AT THE UTAH CAPITOL

The protest movement in Utah did not just show up with signs. It showed up with creativity — and with an image so striking it went viral nationwide.

Mermaids at the Utah Capitol protest the 40,000-acre Stratos data center in Box Elder County on May 14, 2026. ￼

Protesters dressed as mermaids. At the Utah State Capitol. Protesting a data center that wants to drain Utah’s groundwater.

The symbolism was perfect. Mermaids — creatures of the water — standing on the dry steps of a government building to say: if you drain our water for a data center, there will be nothing left for the creatures that depend on it.

The images went everywhere. And they brought national attention to a fight that had previously been contained to rural Box Elder County.

💪 MORE THAN 600 UTAHNS RALLIED — AND 3,700 FILED FORMAL WATER PROTESTS

The mermaids were just the beginning.

More than 600 people rallied at the Capitol on Saturday afternoon, calling for an end to the proposed data center development in Box Elder County. ￼

Christaline Cornell braved the heat Saturday with her infant son to stand on the steps of the state Capitol and protest the Stratos Project, saying his future is the reason she had to attend. “The water, the food, the planet, the environment — we can’t get that back once we take it away,” the American Fork woman said. ￼

A mother. Standing in the Utah heat. Holding her infant son. Fighting for his future.

And the formal legal resistance was just as powerful. More than 3,700 protests were lodged over water rights for the Box Elder data center. ￼

3,700 formal legal protests. Over water rights. Filed by Utah residents who refused to let their groundwater be taken without a fight.

🦈 KEVIN O’LEARY BLAMED CHINA. UTAH WASN’T BUYING IT

The man behind the Stratos Project is Kevin O’Leary — the Shark Tank investor and television personality. And his response to the wave of public opposition became one of the most talked-about moments of this entire debate.

O’Leary accused China of spreading misinformation and fomenting opposition through social media posts — claiming the resistance to his project was orchestrated by foreign interference rather than genuine Utahn concern.

Data center developer Kevin O’Leary has dismissed critics as outsiders, but attendees emphasized they are from Utah. ￼

Outsiders. That is what O’Leary called the 600 people who stood in the Utah heat. The mother with her infant son. The woman dressed as a mermaid. The father from Cache County whose child balanced on his hip at the Capitol rally.

Utah was not buying it. And the backlash to O’Leary’s China claim made national headlines — with independent researchers and polling data confirming that opposition to data centers in America is overwhelmingly organic, domestic, and growing by the day.

🏛️ THE SPEAKER OF THE HOUSE OWNS LAND NEAR THE PROJECT — AND UTAH IS ASKING WHY

Here is the detail that turned a water fight into a full-blown political scandal.

The protest on Thursday was prompted by Utah Speaker of the House Mike Schultz making a visit to St. George — and the land he owns near the proposed site of the Stratos Project in Box Elder County. ￼

The Speaker of the Utah House of Representatives. Owns land. Near the proposed site. Of the data center he helped fast-track through approval.

Protesters did not just show up to oppose a data center. They showed up to ask their elected leaders a direct question: whose interests are you actually serving?

📉 THE PROJECT SCALED BACK — BUT THE FIGHT IS NOT OVER

Under the enormous weight of public pressure, O’Leary agreed to cut the Stratos data center area in half — from 40,000 acres to approximately 20,000 acres. A second water rights application was filed, triggering a new round of formal protests.

According to the Division of Water Rights, the protest period will be open until June 16, 2026. ￼

June 16. That is in three days. The formal window for Utahns to file legal protests against the Stratos Project’s water rights application closes in 72 hours.

The project is smaller than it was. But it is still moving forward. And Utah is still fighting.

🏛️ AND CONGRESS? CONGRESS IS WATCHING. AND WAITING.

Here is the part of this story that makes every community in America feel abandoned.

The saga that has unfolded in Utah highlights how far Congress is from legislating on the issue. So far, lawmakers are mostly leaving it to localities to figure it out. ￼

Mostly leaving it to localities to figure it out. That is the official position of the United States Congress on one of the most consequential land, water, and energy fights in modern American history.

600 people in the Utah heat. 3,700 formal water protests. Mermaids at the Capitol. A mother holding her infant son. A fight over billions of gallons of groundwater in one of the driest states in America.

And Congress is watching. And waiting.

“You can’t, across the board, act as if every data center project is equal,” EPA Administrator Zeldin said at the Politico Energy Summit. “I’m not going to sit inside of an agency building in Washington, D.C., and say that we know that local community in Georgia or Florida or Arizona or elsewhere, better than everyone there locally.” ￼

Washington is not coming to help. Utah is on its own. And so is every other community in America fighting the same fight.

🔮 WHAT HAPPENS NEXT — AND WHY THE NEXT 72 HOURS MATTER

The formal water rights protest window closes June 16 — in three days. After that date, the legal pathway for Utahns to formally challenge the Stratos Project’s water rights becomes significantly narrower.

A nonprofit has filed a lawsuit challenging not only the Stratos Project itself — but the legal authority of MIDA, the appointed board that approved it — arguing the entire fast-track approval process was unconstitutional.

Utah lawmakers have voted to study the impacts of the Box Elder County data center. Another protest is scheduled for this coming weekend.

The fight is not over. Not even close.

But the clock is ticking. The water rights window closes in 72 hours. And the most powerful government in the world is sitting in Washington — watching. And waiting.

Utah deserves better than that. And so does every American community in the same fight.

This story broke THIS MORNING. June 7, 2026. From the Washington Post — one of the most powerful newspapers in the world.

And it confirms what communities from Nashville to Utah to New York to Louisiana have been saying for two years:

The data center fight is no longer just an environmental story. It is no longer just an energy story. It is no longer just a community story.

It is now an election story. And the politicians who ignored it are running out of time to catch up.

THE TWO MOMS WHO ARE ABOUT TO CHANGE AMERICAN POLITICS

Meet Annette Singh and Annie Cannelongo. Two full-time mothers. Living in Hilliard, Ohio — a suburban community outside Columbus that most people in Washington D.C. have never heard of.

They are not political activists. They are not lobbyists. They are not funded by any organization. They are moms. Who take their children to a park next to an elementary school. A park that sits next to the land where Amazon Web Services just broke ground on a data center campus.

Annette Singh and Annie Cannelongo will vote in November in this midterm battleground with one issue at the top of their minds: data centers. The full-time moms say their fury over the massive computer-filled warehouses has consumed them ever since Amazon Web Services broke ground on a data center site that stretches from the lush playground their kids use close to the elementary school that Singh’s child attends. ￼

Consumed. That is the word the Washington Post used. Not concerned. Not worried. Consumed.

This is what it looks like when a company makes a decision — quietly, without public input, without community notification — that reaches into the daily life of a mother pushing her child on a swing. And she looks up. And realizes that the land next to where her child plays is being turned into an industrial AI facility. And nobody asked her. Nobody told her. Nobody even sent a letter.

That is the moment that creates a voter who is consumed. And consumed voters — in midterm elections — decide who wins and who loses.

AND THE WASHINGTON POST JUST CONFIRMED: DATA CENTERS WILL DECIDE THE 2026 MIDTERMS

Why most politicians are not calling for data center bans despite voters’ anger. ￼

That is the headline. From the Washington Post. Published TODAY.

Not “Why voters are angry about data centers.” The Washington Post already knows voters are angry — that is not news anymore. The news is why politicians are not responding. Why they are not calling for bans. Why they are not answering the phones and emails and text messages flooding their offices.

The answer — which the Post lays out in devastating detail — is money. Campaign contributions. Economic development deals. The revolving door between state government and the tech industry. The billion-dollar tax breaks that local officials negotiated in secret and cannot defend in public.

Politicians know the voters are furious. They are calculating whether the fury will still be there in November. And two moms in Hilliard, Ohio — standing in a park next to an elementary school — just told the Washington Post that yes. It will still be there. It will be the first thing they think about when they walk into the voting booth.

 “VERY SOON — MAYBE EVEN LATER THIS YEAR — WE’LL BE PRODUCING MORE CHIPS THAN WE CAN TURN ON”

This quote — published by Bloomberg THIS WEEK — is the most extraordinary admission in the history of the AI boom. And it came from inside the industry itself.

Artificial intelligence data centers are on the verge of reaching their limits. To meet ballooning demand, chipmakers like Nvidia are churning out ever more powerful chips, requiring a new generation of data centers that will draw many times more power than their predecessors. “Very soon, maybe even later this year, we’ll be producing more chips than we can turn on,” Tesla Inc.’s energy division warned. ￼

More chips than we can turn on. This year. Because there is not enough electricity. Not enough transformers. Not enough grid capacity. Not enough water. Not enough community tolerance.

The boom that was supposed to be unstoppable just admitted — through one of its own industry insiders — that it is approaching the physical limits of what America’s infrastructure can support.

And the communities fighting back — from Hilliard, Ohio to Nashville, Tennessee to Box Elder County, Utah to New York State — are a major reason why.

AND ERIN BROCKOVICH JUST SAID THE MOST IMPORTANT THING OF THE ENTIRE FIGHT — YESTERDAY ON FOX NEWS

Erin Brockovich said she’s received thousands of reports on AI data centers — and the most common concern is transparency. “If data centers are so great, why are they being built in secret?” she asks. ￼

Seven words. That is all it took.

If data centers are so great — why are they being built in secret?

Why the NDAs? Why the shell companies? Why the secret meetings? Why the elected officials who cannot tell their constituents what was discussed? Why the farmers who had to sign a confidentiality agreement to find out who wanted to buy their land? Why the communities that found out about $12 billion projects the same day as a press conference?

If the benefits are as real as the companies claim — if the jobs are real, the tax revenue is real, the economic development is real — then why does every single deal require secrecy? Why does every single community have to fight for basic information that should be public from the moment a permit is filed?

Erin Brockovich — who has built a career on one simple principle: the public has a right to know — just asked the question that 288,000 Nashville petition signers, and 6,615 BrockovichDataCenter.com reporters, and two moms in a Hilliard, Ohio playground are all asking in different ways.

Why the secrets?

AND THE NUMBERS THIS WEEK TELL THE COMPLETE STORY OF WHERE AMERICA STANDS

Let us put the complete picture of this single week in American data center history in one place:

288,000 people signed the Nashville Zoo petition in 5 days. The Nashville Metro Council votes on a data center moratorium THIS Tuesday.

New York passed the first statewide data center freeze in American history on Thursday.

Kevin O’Leary was forced to cut his Utah Stratos Project from 40,000 to 20,000 acres after community and political pressure.

Virginia Beach permanently banned all new large-scale data centers.

Amazon’s own engineers stood in Seattle City Hall and called their company’s AI expansion an approach that will cause “staggering damage to democracy, to our jobs, and to the earth.”

“In a month, 3,862 residents submitted reports. The map now has 2,716 pins and represents 49 states,” Erin Brockovich wrote on May 27, 2026. ￼

49 states. 2,716 pins. 288,000 petition signers. 6,615 personal reports. One statewide freeze. One permanent city ban. One Shark Tank star cut in half. One zoo with 3,000 animals and a 50th clouded leopard cub.

And two moms in Hilliard, Ohio who told the Washington Post that data centers will be the first thing on their mind when they vote in November.

AND HERE IS WHAT HAPPENS NEXT — THIS WEEK AND BEYOND

Tuesday June 10: Nashville Metro Council votes on data center moratorium. The most watched local vote in America right now.

By end of June: Governor Hochul must decide whether to sign or veto New York’s historic data center freeze.

June 23: Utah Republican primary — where the Stratos Project and Kevin O’Leary’s data center is the defining campaign issue in the Senate President’s race.

November 2026: Midterm elections. Where two moms in Hilliard, Ohio — and millions of Americans like them — will vote with data centers at the top of their minds.

The fight that started in town halls and commission meetings and online petitions is moving to the ballot box. And no politician — regardless of party, regardless of how much they have accepted from the tech industry — can ignore 288,000 signatures and two full-time moms on the front page of the Washington Post.

Here is the bottom line of June 7, 2026:

America has reached the moment in the data center fight when the political system can no longer pretend it is not happening. When the Washington Post puts two Ohio moms on its front page. When Erin Brockovich asks on Fox News why these projects are built in secret. When Amazon’s own engineers stand in city hall and call their company’s approach damaging to democracy. When a state legislature passes a historic freeze and a city permanently bans new facilities — all in the same week.

This is not a protest movement anymore. It is not a grassroots campaign. It is not a fringe concern.

It is American democracy doing exactly what it is supposed to do. Voters deciding what happens in their communities. Politicians being forced to respond. Companies being held accountable.

The clouded leopard cubs are counting on it. The moms in Ohio are voting on it. And 288,000 Americans — and counting — have already said where they stand.

The controversy surrounding the Stratos data center project in Utah escalated dramatically after billionaire investor Kevin O’Leary publicly suggested that local Utah activists and political consultants opposing or questioning the project could be acting as proxies for Chinese interests.

The claim immediately drew backlash because of the contrast at the center of the accusation: the people being singled out including members of Elevate Strategies and other critics, are Utah residents born, raised, and working in the state. Their stated concerns have focused on issues such as electrical grid demands, environmental impacts, water use, growth planning, and transparency surrounding the project. Yet they found themselves portrayed as part of a larger foreign-influence narrative.

Critics of O’Leary’s comments argue that the accusations resembled a conspiracy theory more than a fact-based argument. The irony, they say, is difficult to ignore: a Canadian billionaire who lives in Florida and reportedly has significant financial interests tied to the project was accusing local Utah natives of secretly serving a foreign government. Rather than addressing the substance of the concerns being raised, opponents argue the conversation shifted toward questioning the loyalty and motives of people who actually live in the communities affected.

The dispute has since become larger than the data center itself. Supporters of the activists see it as a debate over whether local residents should be able to question large projects without being labeled enemies or foreign agents. The controversy transformed what began as a discussion about infrastructure and development into a highly public clash over influence, power, and credibility.

The Stratos Project, a massive data center planned for Box Elder County, has run up against equally massive public opposition.

A panel of local journalists joins us to help make sense of the debate.

Tune in to the full conversation now at RadioWest.org, YouTube or wherever else you get podcasts.

Utah just approved one of the largest AI data center projects in the world — a 40,000 acre “Stratos” campus in Box Elder County that could eventually use more electricity than the entire state currently consumes.

Supporters say it could bring jobs, tax revenue, and make the U.S. more competitive in AI and tech. But thousands of residents are protesting over concerns about water usage, air pollution, rising energy demand, noise, and long-term environmental damage in an already dry region.

The project is expected to be powered largely by natural gas and built in phases, while state officials now face growing pressure to prove it won’t hurt Utah families, local wildlife, or the Great Salt Lake.

This isn’t just about Utah anymore. It’s becoming a national debate over how far AI infrastructure should go — and who pays the price for it.

A Shark Tank investor just got a three-person county commission to approve one of the largest data centers ever built and the people who actually live there found out about it the same way you did.

The “Stratos Project” in Box Elder County, Utah is a 40,000-acre AI data center campus backed by Kevin O’Leary. That’s roughly the size of Washington D.C., sitting just north of the Great Salt Lake. The county’s total population is about 65,000 people. Nobody asked them.

When residents showed up to the commission meeting to protest, commissioners listened to the public comment, then literally walked out of the room and approved it via livestream while the crowd watched on a screen. One commissioner told the audience to “grow up.” Another said the vote wasn’t about the data center it was about “personal property rights.” That’s the whole explanation they got.

Here’s what’s being built a facility that will consume 9 gigawatts of power more than double everything the entire state of Utah uses in a year running entirely on natural gas. That alone would increase Utah’s total emissions by 50%. It would also require 16.6 billion gallons of water annually, drawn from tributaries that feed the Great Salt Lake, which is already at near-record low levels. The shrinking lake already creates toxic dust storms across the Salt Lake valley. This project would accelerate that.

The approval was fast-tracked through something called MIDA (the Military Installation Development Authority) a state entity created to support Hill Air Force Base that functions as its own municipality, bypassing normal zoning and public input processes entirely. It also hands developers an 80% property tax cut and slashes energy taxes from 6% to half a percent. The whole thing went from an initial meeting with the governor in January to county approval in May.

When residents pushed back on the water rights application, nearly 4,000 people filed formal protests with the Utah Division of Water Rights. The application was quietly withdrawn on May 7. That’s a real win but the project itself is still moving forward.

O’Leary’s response to the protests was to claim on social media that more than 90% of demonstrators were paid to show up and bused in from out of state. The Salt Lake Tribune investigated and found no evidence of that.

This is what the AI buildout looks like on the ground. Not the glossy press releases about national competitiveness and job creation the reality of a nine-figure project that transforms a rural community’s water supply, air quality, and landscape, approved in a back room while locals watched on a screen and were told to grow up.

Dear State Engineer,

My name is name, and I reside at address. I submit this as a formal protest of Change Application a54385 associated with Water Right 13-4148, pursuant to Utah Code §§ 73-3-3 and 73-3-8.

I also formally request to be granted standing as a protestant and request that this matter be set for a hearing.

This protest is based on the application’s failure to satisfy statutory requirements and the substantial risk it poses to public welfare, water sustainability, and interconnected hydrologic systems across the State of Utah.

---

LEGAL AND FACTUAL BASIS FOR PROTEST

1. Statutory Prohibition on Impairment (Utah Code § 73-3-3)
The State Engineer may not approve a change application if it will impair vested or existing rights. The scale of proposed industrial water use associated with this application presents a high likelihood of direct or cumulative impairment through depletion, altered timing, and system-wide drawdown.

Utah’s hydrologic systems are interconnected; impacts in one basin can propagate regionally. Approval without definitive proof of no impairment would violate the statutory standard.

---

2. Mandatory Denial if Detrimental to Public Welfare (Utah Code § 73-3-8)
The State Engineer is required to reject applications that are detrimental to the public welfare. This is not discretionary.

The proposed allocation of water for a hyperscale industrial data facility raises profound public welfare concerns, including:

- Long-term depletion of already over-allocated water resources
- Prioritization of industrial consumption over agricultural, municipal, and ecological needs
- Increased stress on statewide water systems during prolonged drought conditions

Given current water scarcity, approving new large-scale industrial consumption is fundamentally inconsistent with protecting public welfare.

---

3. Cumulative Impacts to the  and Statewide Risk
Utah is experiencing a documented and ongoing decline in Great Salt Lake levels. Scientific and policy discussions have repeatedly identified reduced inflows as a critical driver.

Large-scale new consumptive uses—especially at the scale proposed—must be evaluated in terms of cumulative basin-wide impacts.

Continued decline of the Great Salt Lake is associated with exposure of lakebed sediments containing arsenic and other heavy metals. This creates a credible and serious risk of toxic dust events affecting air quality, agriculture, ecosystems, and public health across northern Utah.

Failure to rigorously evaluate and prevent contributions to this outcome constitutes a failure to protect public welfare.

---

4. Beneficial Use and Anti-Waste Doctrine (Utah Code § 73-1-3)
All water in Utah is subject to the principle of beneficial use without waste.

Allocating a substantial volume of water to a hyperscale data center—particularly one of extraordinary land and resource scale—raises legitimate questions as to whether this represents the highest and best beneficial use of limited water resources in an arid state.

Where competing needs include food production, municipal supply, and ecological stability, the burden must be high to justify such allocation.

---

5. Inadequate Information and Need for Full Technical Review
Given the magnitude of this proposal, approval without comprehensive analysis would be arbitrary and inconsistent with the State Engineer’s duty of care.

At minimum, the following must be required before any consideration of approval:

- Full hydrologic modeling, including cumulative and long-term impacts
- Basin-wide and interconnected system analysis
- Demonstration of no impairment under worst-case drought conditions
- Detailed accounting of consumptive use, return flows, and mitigation measures
- Public transparency and opportunity for meaningful review

Absent this, the application is incomplete and should be denied.

---

REQUEST FOR RELIEF

Based on the foregoing, I respectfully and urgently request that the State Engineer:

1. Deny Change Application a54385 in its current form;
2. Alternatively, require comprehensive environmental, hydrologic, and public welfare analysis prior to any approval;
3. Formally recognize this protest and grant me standing as a protestant;
4. Set this matter for a hearing so that evidence and public concerns may be fully evaluated on the record.

---

Given the scale of this proposal and the severity of potential impacts, anything less than rigorous scrutiny and full public process would be inadequate.

Please confirm receipt of this protest and notify me of all future proceedings, hearings, or decisions related to this application.
